text: You get a string s and a list of words, wordDict. Add spaces to s so every piece is a dictionary word. Return all the sentences you can make, in any order.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I cut s into pieces, every piece must be in the dictionary, and I return every way to do that, with single spaces between the words. Is that right? And a word can be used more than once, like apple twice in pine apple pen apple?
Yes, words can repeat. And if there's no way to cut it, return an empty list.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
The string length is at most twenty. Up to a thousand words, each at most ten letters. All lowercase, all words unique. And the total answer size won't go over ten to the fifth.

Okay. So n is tiny, but the answer can still be big. That tells me two things. First, I really do have to list every sentence, so the output size is a floor on the time. Second, there's a different danger: inputs where the search does a lot of work and finds nothing. Let me run through the example. Cats and dog, with cat, cats, and, sand, dog: from the start I can take cat or cats, and each leftover splits one way, so I get cats and dog, and cat sand dog. That matches. And cats-and-og gives an empty list. Here's the sneaky part: sand is a real word, but after it the leftover is o g, a dead end. So a path can look good for a while and still fail at the very end.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every set of cut positions — two to the n minus one ways — and check each one. It's correct, but blind: it builds full cuts even when the first piece is already not a word. This problem reminds me of partition backtracking: at index start, pick where the next word ends, check it, go deeper, then undo. It also reminds me of the yes-or-no version, can it be split at all, which is a simple DP. I think I can use that yes-or-no DP to prune this search. So my plan is two steps: first, plain backtracking; then add a pruning table so I never walk into a dead end.

Here's the plan. One: the search tries every end from start; if the piece is a word, it adds it, recurses, and undoes. Two: canBreak of i says whether the suffix from i can be fully split, filled from the right. Three: in the search, skip any end where canBreak is false — that cut can never finish, so I don't even look up the word. One thing worth flagging — the direction matters. The usual yes-or-no DP is a prefix table: can I get here. My search already got here; it needs: can I get from here to the end. A prefix table keeps the answers correct but prunes nothing. There's a trade-off: memoizing each suffix's sentences is also fast on dead ends, but it copies lists of partial sentences. Pruning keeps one path string. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Start with the plain version, then the pruned one.

Alright, let me code this up. First, the plain backtracking. The search saves the path when start reaches the end; otherwise it tries every end, skips pieces that aren't words, appends the word with a space if needed, recurses, and resizes the path back.

One thing worth flagging — the undo step. I save the old length before I add the space and the word, so resizing back removes both. If I only cut off the word's length, the space would stay behind: on double a, with words a and double a, the second answer comes out as a, space, double a, instead of just double a. Two more small guards. The loop goes up to and including n, because the last word has to reach the end; with strictly less than, the single letter a returns an empty list. And the empty-path check stops a leading space. Now the pruned version: same search, plus the canBreak table, and the loop only goes up to the longest word length.

That matches the plan. One thing worth flagging — canBreak of n equals true is the base case. It's not optional. Without it, no index can ever become true, so every input returns an empty list. Also, I check canBreak of end before I build the substring and look in the set. That cheap check skips the expensive part.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Cats and dog on the pruned version, expected two sentences; canBreak is true only at zero, three, four, seven and ten. The row that matters is the search from three: it only tries ends four and seven, the true spots. s fails the dictionary check, sand works, and seven only tries ten. Seven calls, like plain, but dictionary checks drop from twenty-nine to seven, plus fourteen to build the table. On cats-and-og, canBreak of zero is false, so it returns empty with no search call. Let's also test with corner cases. The single letter a returns a, catching the strictly-less-than bug. Double a checks the undo. Nineteen a's then a b, words up to four a's: zero answers, yet plain backtracking makes three hundred six thousand calls, about ten milliseconds. Pruning makes zero.
What if you used the prefix table you mentioned?

It still gives correct answers, because the search checks every word anyway. But it prunes nothing. On that nineteen a's plus b input it still makes all three hundred six thousand calls. The prefix table says I could reach this spot. The search is already standing there, so that's no news. The useful question is can I finish from here, and only the suffix table answers it.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity for the pruned version has two parts. Building canBreak is n times L squared, where L is the longest word: n starts, L ends each, L per substring. The search is output-sensitive: every node I visit has canBreak true, so it leads to at least one sentence. The space complexity is linear besides the answer: the table, the recursion depth, and one path. The output itself can be exponential, so nothing beats that; plain backtracking is two to the n times n, and pays it even with zero answers. Oh, one more thing — pruning isn't magic when almost every branch works. Twenty a's with words a and double a gives ten thousand nine hundred forty-six sentences; all three versions finish within a few milliseconds of each other, because writing the output is the real cost.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You built the plain version first, then showed with a real input — three hundred six thousand calls for zero answers — why it needs pruning. You saw that the pruning table has to be suffix-based, and explained why the prefix table prunes nothing. And you were honest about the limits: when the output is huge, the output size sets the cost, not the search. Good work.
